content.p: In the second week of January 2021, hundreds of Venezuelan police officers moved into La Vega, a hillside district in the southwest of Caracas, and over the next few days at least 23 people died. Independent media and human rights groups called it a massacre. Relatives said their sons, nephews and brothers had been seized in their homes or in the street and shot, and then presented as having died in a confrontation with police. The authorities, according to the human rights group Provea, said the deaths had occurred in clashes with elite police units.

Provea and the monitoring project Lupa por la Vida described it as the deadliest single police operation of its kind in Venezuela in half a century. Justicia y Verdad, a news site that reported on those groups' counts, called it the deadliest in the history of the country's so-called citizen security operations. Amnesty International judged that at least 14 of the deaths were probable extrajudicial executions. A year after the raid, Provea said that no progress in any investigation was known.

Reports from the time said the authorities had made no statement on the events, so the figure came mostly from monitors, journalists and families. The Caracas morgue at Bello Monte became the place where it was assembled. On Monday 11 January 2021, El Estímulo reported relatives gathering there, and wrote that the operation on the Friday and Saturday had left 24 dead; the same article said that early counts had ranged from 18 to 22 and that only eight bodies had so far been identified by their families.

Caracas Chronicles reported in its 12 January summary that Provea counted at least 23 people dead in the police operation of 8 January. That number, 23, became the one most often used by Venezuelan rights groups. The US State Department, in its report on 2022, wrote of "at least 24" people killed. Amnesty International counted at least 14 deaths during an operation it said lasted until 9 January, and added reports of ten more fatal victims of police action. The UN fact-finding mission on Venezuela, speaking in March 2021, put the raid within a wider toll of 200 people killed by police that year, and dated the La Vega operation 7 to 9 January.

The start date also varies. Amnesty said that neighbours had denounced a police presence from 6 January and set the period of the deaths between 6 and 9 January. Most Venezuelan sources, including Provea, date the main operation to 8 January 2021.

According to Amnesty, as many as 650 officers of the Venezuelan security forces were in La Vega parish on 8 January, ostensibly because of clashes between gangs and the police. Provea reported that the UN mission also spoke of 650 agents, drawn from official sources. The units named differed from report to report. Amnesty referred to the Special Action Forces, known as FAES, and other members of the Bolivarian National Police. Provea listed FAES, the police's criminal investigations directorate and its Special Tactical Operations Unit. The Justicia y Verdad summary named mixed commissions of FAES, the national forensic and criminal investigation agency CICPC and the National Guard.

Amnesty said it verified nine videos filmed on 8 and 9 January. One showed a convoy of police vehicles heading south along Avenida O'Higgins toward the area; others showed heavily armed police on the streets, gunshots in the distance, and a police pick-up leaving La Vega with what appeared to be bodies in the back.

The stated aim of the operation, as Provea reported it, was to confront the "El Coqui" gang, which controls Cota 905, the neighbouring district. Provea wrote that, days earlier, the gang had reportedly taken several sectors of La Vega to extend its domain. A resident, Mailyn Useche, told El Estímulo that she had heard the police were mounting a special operation for that reason.

Outside the morgue on 11 January, relatives repeated the same phrases to reporters: that the dead were not criminals, and that a brother had only gone out to buy cigarettes. El Estímulo's report and Provea's later accounts both recorded testimony of arrests followed by killing.

Mailyn Useche said her nephew, Richard Chili, was in his room watching football on a computer when officers knocked. According to her, they questioned him, photographed him in shorts and without a shirt, dressed him, covered his face and took him away. She said that a photograph later showed him dead on the floor. Provea lists a Richard Alejandro Chile Cabello, 20, a car wash employee, among the dead.

Provea's year-end report described two brothers, Ángel Jesús and Giovani Daboín Palma Martínez, aged 27 and 32. The report said they were detained without a judicial order and shot in their home by nine officers of the Bolivarian National Police. Ángel was hit first in the leg, it said, and then in the chest, and he called for help while officers did not allow relatives to help him. Giovani, it said, was shot twice elsewhere in the house, once in the forehead and once in the chest, though the death certificate does not record the head wound.

Another victim named by relatives was Luis Alejandro Ramírez Muñoz, 22. His aunt told El Estímulo he had worked for more than two years as a computer technician at Sarem. She said photos circulating on social media had shown him alive, in shorts and without a shirt, before he appeared dead in different clothes. El Estímulo noted that official records showed a police entry for him, dated December 2018, for unlawful carrying of a firearm. The same article reported a police source's claim that all the dead had records, and noted that, in the view of some, a record makes such killings seem justified.

Several families, according to Provea, said officers took belongings and in one case threatened relatives not to report. Provea also reported residents' claims that armed people in black, whom they took for pro-government colectivos, had been seen in the parish the night before. Provea said the families told it that some victims were killed inside homes on several streets and others while walking.
content.h2: The official line and its echoes
content.p: The Atlantic Council's Digital Forensic Research Lab wrote on 13 January that the circumstances of the operation remained unclear because the Maduro government had yet to release an official statement. Pro-government outlets La Tabla and La Iguana, it said, described La Vega as peaceful afterwards and wrote that 15 alleged gang members and "two innocents" supposedly hit by stray bullets were among the dead. The freelance journalist whom La Iguana quoted, Roman Camacho, spoke of 13 "criminals" without naming a source. FAES commander Miguel Domínguez shared the La Iguana link on 8 January and posted the next day that FAES provided "security and protection" in La Vega, but gave no further account.
The same analysis found signs of inauthentic behaviour among Twitter accounts amplifying pro-government posts about the operation; one account had posted 5,139 times between 9 and 12 January.

Amnesty said that, as far as it knew, there had been no report of a death or injury among the security forces. Provea made the same point in general terms, saying that very few officers are hurt or killed in raids on poor districts. Provea added that the official version of clashes is contradicted by the statistics.

Amnesty obtained images that appeared to show 14 of the dead. An external forensic pathologist, it said, confirmed that seven bodies had gunshot wounds over the heart and two more a single wound immediately above it; two had a single wound to the head. Amnesty argued that the location and number of the wounds made the official crossfire account "even less credible".

It also described a pattern drawn from families' testimony in earlier cases. Security forces enter homes without warrants, immobilise a young person, shoot him once or twice in the chest or head, then alter the scene, simulate a clash or move the body, and classify the death as "resistance to authority". Zair Mundaray, a former official of the public prosecutor's office quoted by El Estímulo, called this a common practice among police bodies. El Estímulo added that, among the images circulating, the wounds were in the chest, one or two each.

Amnesty did not say it had proved who fired in each case. Its language was that there were solid reasons to believe that at least 14 deaths were likely extrajudicial executions, which might constitute crimes against humanity.
content.h2: Geneva, and a year of silence
content.p: In March 2021 Marta Valinas, who led the UN fact-finding mission, told the Human Rights Council that the 200 killings by police since January included people who died in the La Vega operation. Her words, as MercoPress reported them: "Our preliminary investigations indicate that at least some of those killed were victims of extrajudicial executions." The mission also said it had received reports that authorities had not released death certificates, had charged fees for autopsies and had handed over bodies in closed coffins with instructions that they not be opened.

Venezuela's ambassador in Geneva, Héctor Constant Rosales, said the mission was again presenting "politicized information with no balance and fairness". The foreign ministry later rejected the mission's "false accusations". The United States and Brazil raised the case at the council; the US chargé d'affaires, Mark Cassayre, called it a "massacre", and a US statement said that Amnesty had reported that FAES members had killed more than 14 people.

Provea, in May 2021, noted that four months on neither Attorney General Tarek William Saab nor Ombudsman Alfredo Ruiz had said anything, and that the names of the dead had not been officially released. Justicia y Verdad reported the same silence and relatives' helplessness.

On the first anniversary, Provea, the Centro Gumilla and Lupa por la Vida published a 36-page report saying that no progress in investigations was known and that, to their knowledge, no inquiry had been opened. It named FAES director José Miguel Domínguez, who they said led the operation, and Interior Minister Carmen Meléndez as among those who should be investigated, together with other participating officials. These are the groups' calls for inquiry, not findings by any court. They also asked that FAES be dissolved and that families be compensated. A parish priest, Alfredo Infante of the Centro Gumilla, said most of the victims were neither in the confrontation nor tied to gangs.

The US State Department's report on 2022 recorded "some progress" in the investigation: non-governmental groups reported that FAES officers had been identified as potentially responsible for the deaths of four of the victims, but there were no convictions.
